I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

Here lies the key to everything we shall hear about theophany as the resolution, through inward tawhid, of the impasse of abstract monotheism. There is identity within difference between the One who reveals Himself and the one to whom He is revealed.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

Among all human experiences there is one, and only one, through which this identity can be lived and truly known: human love for a beautiful person. The form of love in question is not, of course, directed toward a social end, such as founding a family. Through its own discipline, it has freed itself from the possessive bodily impulses of the nafs ammara, whose unchecked force we see at work in outward social life. It is essentially the soul shaken and carried beyond itself by a theophany—by the revelation of divine Beauty in a beautiful human being.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

Ibn Arabi taught this devotion to beauty; in Iran it was practiced above all by Ruzbihan and those of his school. Ruzbihan distinguishes the pious worshippers and mystical ascetics (zohhad) for whom human love did not mark the beginning of the spiritual Path from those for whom human love was the first step toward divine love: the khawass al-mahabba, whom I have proposed to call the “Faithful of Love,” to bring out their affinity with the Fedeli d'amore of Dante's age.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

There is a further point. Inward tawhid affirms an identity: the divine Being is at once love, the lover, and the beloved. Only the experience of human love for a beautiful person can lead us to understand this identity, to make it real within ourselves, because only there, at the furthest perfection of such love, can that identity be lived. This is the point reached by Majnun, the legendary lover, when he knows himself to be Layla. He is so completely absorbed in her image, so entirely inwardly present to her, that when someone asks his name, he answers: “Layla.”
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

Human Eros and divine love, then, are not opposed. Divine love can be discovered and experienced only through human love. And this is because Layla's beauty is none other than divine Beauty, of which it is a visible manifestation. Her beauty is a sacred sign (ayat), a sacramentum. To reach this summit, of course, everything ordinarily and casually called love must be utterly transfigured. This transfiguration demands a spiritual struggle, a secret personal effort of which pious devotees cannot even conceive: they see nothing in it but “aestheticism.”
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

Yet it was precisely this transfiguration that all the minstrels of Iran's religion of love affirmed—Ahmad Ghazali, Awhad al-Din Kermani, Fakhr al-Din Iraqi, and so many others. One great figure among them, however, had until now remained almost unknown, together with a body of work long left unpublished: Ruzbihan Baqli of Shiraz. It is this work, the very image of a life if ever a work deserved that name, whose stages I wish to trace here. Through it, we may understand the distinctively Iranian phenomenon of a mystical religion of human beauty, in which human love initiates the soul into divine love and gives that love the form of an inward, esoteric Islam.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

Ruzbihan's own interpretation of our Quranic verse tells us what is at stake. He understands it as a call back to one's origin, addressed to the Holy Spirit that constitutes the spiritual individuality of the human being. It is addressed to the one who, from beginning to end, has turned toward no vision but the vision of God: to the soul content with Him through Him, and therefore pleasing in His sight by virtue of a choice made before eternity. What makes this Path distinctive, however, is that the vision of God does not require turning away from a created being.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

Instead, in the very sight of that being's beauty, one sees divine Beauty directly—not by deduction, but immediately, without intermediary or pause. As a disciple of Ibn Arabi declares in commenting on the same verse, upon one who reaches this state “the Sakina, the Peace, has descended; he has been illuminated by the light of certainty, and in God he has found rest from restlessness.” Ruzbihan is an outstanding representative of this spiritual path. Perhaps he was the first to express it with such clarity and to gather such testimony to it.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

Among Ruzbihan's surviving works is a document of extraordinary visionary richness: a Spiritual Diary, a record of his inner life, his dreams, and his visions. Almost the only comparable account is one left by the great Central Asian Sufi Najm al-Din Kubra, or, in the West, Swedenborg's Diarium spirituale. Ruzbihan's doctrinal writings continually return to events recounted in his Spiritual Diary. One might say that this shaykh never advances a teaching that is not grounded in his own experience.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

And however strange those experiences may seem, we must beware of speaking of schizophrenia. In mystics of his kind, it is striking how clearly consciousness distinguishes between real events undergone in visionary states and real events undergone while awake. The recurring desire throughout his spiritual life is the longing for vision: the vision denied to Moses but granted to the Prophet of Islam. This is why the Prophet appears to Sufis as the Sayyed-e Ashiqan, the “Prince of the Faithful of Love.”
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

The gift of such vision is a theophany; but theophany is given only in and through a created being, without the divine becoming incarnate in that being. It enters “as an image enters a mirror.” Ruzbihan will be constantly concerned to dispel the misunderstanding sustained by the hostility, or the inability to understand, of the guardians of legalistic orthodoxy.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

A theophany (tajalli) is not an incarnation (holul). The two notions could be brought together only if incarnation were understood as taking the form of the human body, in the full perfection of that form's beauty, rather than assuming its material substance, its “flesh.” This is no doubt what gives so many Sufi statements their “Docetic” quality: they speak of an appearing in human form without a material incarnation.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul
Yet this view is nothing less than a realism of the spiritual.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

Ruzbihan does not hesitate to describe himself as a malamati: one of those Sufis who do not fear the disapproval of official religious conformity, and may even seek it out, wearing blame like a disguise that conceals the purity of their inner face. In this sense Ruzbihan may be regarded as a forerunner of another famous son of Shiraz, one of Iran's greatest mystical poets: Hafez. He even helps us clear up the misunderstandings of Hafez that have arisen in the West. In Iran, Sufis read Hafez's Divan as a mystical Bible.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

Yet in the West people have asked whether its words should be taken literally or mystically. Ruzbihan would answer that the question is wrongly framed, because it assumes a choice between denying and accepting a material incarnation. There is another possibility, which he calls by the technical term amphiboly (iltibas): the presence of two meanings at once, which can be mistaken for one another. No theophany takes place without a moment of this ambiguity.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

Whoever understands it has found peace. Such a person no longer fears some divine deception, and no longer seeks refuge either in literal faith or in the material certainty of sensory facts. Only one certainty remains: the certainty given by seeing the invisible and hearing the inaudible. Once the secret of their hidden agreement is deciphered, the ambiguity that colors everything in this world proves to be nothing other than the correspondence of all things with one another.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul
Indeed, our two terms, amphiboly and symbolism, come from the same Greek root.

Ruzbihan was born in 522/1128 at Fasa (or Pasa), a town some 140 kilometers from Shiraz, in Fars—the region known as Persis, Persia in the strict sense of the name. He died in Shiraz in 606/1209. The sixth century of the Islamic calendar, the twelfth century of the Common Era, nearly coincides with the span of his long life, and is of decisive importance in Iran's spiritual history. Unfortunately, the great events of that history are rarely considered alongside contemporary events in the West.

Our understanding of human cultures still has far to go before we can imagine a comprehensive account of human consciousness that neglects no period and no region. It was in this twelfth century that Suhrawardi revived the philosophy of ancient Iran, its doctrine of Light. It was in 1164, in northwestern Iran, that the proclamation of the Great Resurrection at Alamut established reformed Ismailism as a spiritual Islam, a religion of personal salvation.

Having thus rediscovered the path and meaning of its origins, Ismailism would survive the Mongol upheaval by assuming, without any usurpation, the cloak of Sufism. In Transoxiana, another great spiritual master, Najm al-Din Kubra, gave Sufism a new direction, turning it toward attentive contemplation of the colored lights perceived by the mystic during spiritual states. His school would produce illustrious disciples: Najm al-Din Razi, Aziz al-Din Nasafi, Ala al-Dawla Simnani, and others. In that same century, at Nishapur in Khurasan, Farid al-Din Attar composed his magnificent mystical epics in Persian.

These are the events that help us place Ruzbihan of Shiraz within the spiritual world of his time. He left this world a few years after Ibn Arabi departed his native Andalusia to become, for the rest of his life, a pilgrim in the East, where he spread a mystical philosophy of incomparable power. Ibn Arabi's teaching on love has much in common with Ruzbihan's. We are still far from being able to reconstruct the origins and development of this Sufi spirituality. In any case, that is not our task here.

We are concerned with Ruzbihan's own life, both personal and exemplary. He expresses his experience sometimes in Arabic, sometimes in Persian of remarkable individuality, beauty, and difficulty. His writings disclose the secret of a soul that found peace after confronting the severity of tawhid, the assertion of divine unity, and its double danger. This is the dilemma that haunts Islamic scholastic thought: in trying to avoid assimilating the divine to created beings (tashbih), one may end by reducing God to an abstraction (ta'til).

Only access to inward tawhid can escape that trap. Ruzbihan found such access through a mystical experience pushed to its furthest limit, one that goes beyond the Platonic echoes recognizable in his writings. It goes beyond them because, at its heart, it is a mystical verification of prophetic religion itself. And that verification presupposes a perception of the prophetic meaning of beauty, expressed in one of the favorite sayings of the Sufism of the Faithful of Love: “God is beautiful, and He loves beauty.”

Beauty is not simply one divine Attribute among others. It is the essential Attribute. God Himself is therefore both the source and the reality of Eros, and two ways of desecrating it must be ruled out: the libertinism that profanes love, and the asceticism that denies it, whether through calculation or an ingrained cult of misery.

To follow Ruzbihan's spiritual life, let us recount a few episodes from his extraordinary Diary. It reveals that from childhood he possessed both exceptional emotional sensitivity and an exceptional gift for visions, as though the solid wall separating ordinary humanity from the invisible world had never existed for him. His certainty came from this experience, not from the construction of theories. He knew through experience the presence of gentle and noble beings, beautiful figures, angels, prophets, and saints, in whose company the shaykh of Shiraz lived.

At the center—or summit—of all this stood the repeated vision of the One who is by nature forever invisible: the One who refused Himself to Moses, yet of whom the Prophet of Islam could testify, “I saw my God in the most beautiful of forms.” This paradox is affirmed and lived throughout Ruzbihan's experience, for love in its fullest sense can be directed only toward a being with a distinct personhood and face.

God, loved in this way, must take on the form of the eternal Companion, the “Witness in Heaven.” (Here, as so often, Sufism recreates a teaching about the Imam without naming it.) To discover inward tawhid is precisely to resolve a contradiction that philosophy or theology, when it thinks only in terms of objects, cannot overcome: the contradiction between God's transcendence beyond all personhood and these personal manifestations, each suited to the soul that loves. The solution is the very secret of theophanies, and initiation into that secret is nothing other than initiation into the divine mystery of love. For that mystery is the identity of love, lover, and beloved.

Ruzbihan wrote his Spiritual Diary at a friend's request. He was then fifty-five years old; the mysterious experiences, he tells us, had begun when he was fifteen. The interval is long, but he tries to recover his memories as closely as possible. He writes: “I was born among ignorant people, people lost in drunkenness and error, coarse and vulgar, like startled donkeys fleeing from a lion (Quran 74:51).

“I had reached the age of three when this question arose in my heart: Where is your God, and the God of all creatures? There was a mosque beside the entrance to our house. One day I saw some young boys and asked them: Do you know your God? They answered: People say He has neither feet nor hands. They had heard their parents say that God Most High has no limbs or bodily organs.

“After asking this question, I was overwhelmed with emotion and began to run. Something happened to me like the sudden flashes that come from remembering, or the unexpected glimpses that open up in meditation; in truth, I did not understand what was happening.” Perhaps we can begin to understand it.

On one side stood abstract monotheism and the philosophy of rational theism, united in affirming a divinity beyond all forms, descriptions, and personal attributes. On the other stood a young mystic who already sensed that the eternal Beloved could not be without a face—a face whose secret, once revealed and once it had shaken him to the depths, he would have to conceal with reverence.

“From the age of seven,” Ruzbihan continues, “my heart fell in love with the practice of dhikr”—the remembrance of God—“and with devotion. I began to seek my secret (sirr) and to learn its ways. Then passionate love (ishq) blossomed in my heart, and I felt my heart melt in that love. Throughout this time I lived in deep longing, for even then my heart had plunged into the ocean of remembrance of my eternal pre-existence and into the fragrance of the heavenly world.

“Later, sudden intuitions of fleeting ecstasies began to flower within me. There was no physical trembling, though a certain sweetness filled my heart, while tears streamed from my eyes... I saw every being as a beautiful face; and as they appeared to me in this way, I felt drawn toward particular kinds of retreat, toward intimate prayers (monajat), acts of devotion, and pious visits to the tombs of the most eminent Sufi shaykhs.”

Then came the event of adolescence that would determine the course of his whole life. Ruzbihan was fifteen. Seeing all beings as beautiful faces already shows us the quality that will dominate his mature inner life.

But another feature reveals the Sufi's deepest aspiration: a vocation to the prophetic state, the state of the nabi, or prophet. The adolescent hears an inward voice assuring him of this calling. He resists: it seems to him that the physical weaknesses of ordinary humanity cannot be reconciled with the state of a prophet. Besides, has he not been taught that there will be no prophet after Muhammad? Certainly.

But is Muhammad's heavenly ascent not the model for the experience the mystic seeks to repeat? And is the spiritual interpretation of the Quran not a continual renewal of prophetic interpretation? This problem, which arose and was resolved within Islam through Shiism itself, also lies at the heart of Sufism. That is why, in practice, a study of religious experience should never treat these two spiritual traditions in isolation.

One evening after supper, the young Ruzbihan, who until then had kept a small shop in Shiraz, rises from his place of business and makes his way toward a familiar spot in the nearby desert. Suddenly he hears a gentle voice calling him. He climbs a hill and finds himself before a person of extraordinary beauty, with the appearance of a Sufi shaykh, who says a few words to him about tawhid.

Ruzbihan cannot speak. He barely understands, and is carried beyond his senses. When he comes to himself, part of the night has passed. He returns home, where he remains until morning overcome by emotion and unrest, sighing and weeping. “I was astonished and shaken,” he writes. “Without my willing it, my tongue kept saying: Your forgiveness! Your forgiveness! Then it subsided. It seemed to me that it had lasted for hours and hours. I waited another hour.

“Finally my emotion grew so violent that I threw aside my cashbox and gathered everything in the shop into a bundle. I tore my clothes and went out into the desert. I remained in that state for a year and a half, longing, astonished, weeping, swept away by emotion. Every day brought magnificent visions of ecstasy and sudden visitations from the invisible worlds. During these visions, the heavens and the earth, mountains, deserts, plants—everything appeared to me as pure light. Afterward, I came to know a certain peace.”

We should notice the defining feature of these first events, lived at the threshold of consciousness beyond the ordinary. Just as the universe begins to appear to the adolescent transfigured into beautiful faces, his first personal encounter with a beautiful messenger from the invisible world comes as a shock centered on tawhid, the declaration of monotheistic faith. At first Ruzbihan does not understand what he is told; his later life and teachings will explain it to us.

What is at stake is the very secret of theophanies: how the unity affirmed by tawhid multiplies itself in each of its manifestations while remaining one (1 × 1), and how uncreated Beauty can be seen only in the beautiful faces through which it appears. Through this secret, the “soul at peace” makes “its return to its Lord.” The visions that follow in the Spiritual Diary mark the first stages of his initiation into that return.

At the same time they reveal the archetypal figures that shape the consciousness of an Iranian Sufi. “I remember this, too,” Ruzbihan writes. “I was on the roof terrace of my house when I saw God in the attribute of might and majesty. The whole universe appeared to me as a vast, teeming, brilliant light. Then, from the center of that light, He called to me seven times in Persian: O Ruzbihan!

“I have chosen you for the station of My Friend (walayat); I have chosen you for love. You are My friend, one who loves Me. Give way neither to fear nor to sorrow, for I am your God, and I watch over you in everything you undertake.”

Another event then appears, like a genuine ordeal of initiation lived in a visionary state. “This time it seemed in my vision that I was on the Mountain of the East, and I saw a whole company of angels there. From East to West stretched an immense sea; I could see nothing else. The angels said to me: Enter this sea and swim toward the West. I entered the sea and began to swim.

“When I reached the place where the sun sets, at the hour of its decline... I saw a company of angels on the Mountain of the West, lit by the setting sun. They cried to me: You, over there! Swim on, and do not be afraid. When at last I reached the mountain, they said: No one has crossed this sea except Ali ibn Abi Talib, and you after him.”
Two things stand out in these visionary events of initiation.

First there is the double reference: to walayat, originally a Shiite idea, and to the First Imam of Shiism, who appears here as the exemplary hero of the young initiate. Then there is the setting of the vision itself. The perilous journey toward the setting sun, into the region of Darkness, belongs to the great theme of the Quest for the Source of Life. Two archetypal figures dominate the legend: Alexander and Khizr (Khezr, or Khadir), who is sometimes paired with the prophet Elijah and sometimes identified with him.

Khizr reaches the Source of Life; whoever, like him, succeeds in finding light in the region of Darkness is a disciple of Khizr. Suhrawardi's mystical tales have already introduced us to this figure and his role (see above, Book II, Chapter V). We should add that Khizr's role, and his superiority to the lawgiving prophets—he is Moses' initiator—remain incomprehensible apart from Shiite teachings about prophecy and walayat. Some Shiites have even identified him with the “Hidden Imam.”

Hence his extraordinary role in Sufism. He is the master of all those who receive their initiation directly from him, without contact with any human master and independently of any historical chain of initiation passing through successive generations of a tariqa. He is the master of those who have no outward master: those known in Shiism as the Uwaysis. To be a disciple of Khizr, as so many Sufis have been—and as Suhrawardi teaches in the Tale of the Crimson Archangel—is to become what Khizr became and to do what he did.

Through him, a Sufi receives a direct connection to the heavenly world and its invisible hierarchies, an initiation whose authority and meaning transcend history because they do not depend on the succession of human generations in earthly time. In the deepest sense of the Quest, this is the return of the soul at peace: the attainment of one's own true being, of the divine counterpart of oneself, of which Khizr is one of the great symbols.

Two further visions lead Ruzbihan first to Khizr himself and then to two shaykhs who are the very “image” of the mystical pilgrim and reveal to him the inward rank he has now attained. Having reached the region of Darkness near the “pole,” Ruzbihan, like Khizr, discovers light there—the vision of angels blazing in the light of the setting sun—and finds the Source of Life in the form of luminous water.

Here the initiation received directly from Khizr does not take the form of bestowing the khirqa, the Sufi cloak, as it does in the stories of other Sufis. Instead, it takes the form of eating a fruit. “At that time I knew nothing of the higher sciences of divine wisdom, and then I saw Khizr. He gave me an apple, and I ate part of it.

“Eat it all, he said to me; that is how much I ate. Then it seemed to me that from the Throne to the Pleiades there stretched an immense sea, and I could see nothing else. It was like the radiance of the sun. My mouth opened against my will, and all the contents of that sea of light poured into it. Not a single drop remained that I had not swallowed.”

The next vision completes this stage of initiation. Its symbolic figures express with extraordinary eloquence the fullness of spiritual life Ruzbihan has reached. The whole of creation appears to him enclosed within a house.

Many lamps shed brilliant light inside it, but a wall prevents him from reaching them. He climbs onto the roof terrace of his own house, where he finds two figures of great beauty in whom he recognizes his own image. (We could hardly wish for a clearer illustration of the theme of the image, the heavenly alter ego, developed earlier in connection with the “history” of the seeker of spiritual knowledge: Book II, Chapter VI, sections 1 and 4.) The two figures look like Sufis and smile at him with affection.

The visionary notices a hanging cooking pot. Beneath it burns a subtle, pure, smokeless fire, fed by fragrant herbs. One of the figures then unfolds a cloth, bringing to light a graceful bowl and several loaves of pure wheat bread. He breaks one of the loaves into the bowl and pours over it the contents of the pot: an oil so subtle that it seems to be made of spiritual substance.

The three then share what is almost a meal of communion. “One of them said to me: Do you know what was in the pot? No, I said, I do not. It was oil from the Great Bear, which we had gathered for you. When I came out of my vision, I pondered this, but only after some time did I understand that it referred to the seven poles in the heavenly realm (malakut).

“God had granted me the pure substance of their mystical rank: the rank of the Seven, who are invisibly distributed over the face of the earth. Then I turned my attention toward the Great Bear, and I saw that it formed seven openings through which, all together, God showed Himself (tajalli) to me. My God, I cried, what is this? He answered: These are the seven openings of the Throne.”

Ruzbihan, a disciple of Khizr, now knows that he has taken his place among the seven Abdal, at the summit of the mysterious, invisible hierarchy surrounding the “Pole,” the “Hidden Imam” of the age, without whom earthly life could not continue. The idea of such hierarchies, apparently linked in its origins to an esoteric astrology, pervades the spiritual philosophy of Sufism. It seems so closely bound up with Shiite spiritual knowledge itself that it has again assumed a fundamental role in more recent times, within Shaykhism.

For Ruzbihan, too, this experience of initiation is so decisive that, as he goes on to recount, “every night thereafter I continued watching those openings in the heavens, driven by my love and ardent longing. Then one night I saw that they were open, and I saw God manifesting Himself to me through them. He said: I manifest Myself to you through these openings; they form seven thousand thresholds leading to the threshold of the angelic realm (malakut). And see: I show Myself to you through them all at once.”

“Through them all at once.” In other passages of Ruzbihan's Diary we shall see that here lies the secret of the meeting of unity and multiplicity. Whoever is allowed to penetrate the secret of theophanies understands what the masters mean by the “ordeal of the Veil.” To overcome that ordeal is to hold one's gaze steady, as the Prophet did at his vision by the “lotus tree of the utmost boundary” (53:17): when faced with each theophany, the gaze neither turns aside nor oversteps its limit. These few autobiographical glimpses are enough to suggest the spiritual character of the great mystic of Shiraz.

As we have described the outward circumstances of his life more fully elsewhere, we shall only mention them here: the shaykhs from whom he later received his theological education; his journeys through Iran and Iraq and to Mecca; the crowds of disciples who came from all directions to be initiated by him into the Sufism of the Faithful of Love; and the part played by the khanqah, the Sufi lodge he founded in Shiraz, in the spiritual and social life of southwestern Iran—not only in the shaykh's lifetime, but through his descendants for several generations.

We should nevertheless recount two further episodes that reveal something essential about Ruzbihan himself. It is said that on the day he first took up his duties as a preacher at the mosque in Shiraz, he was passing through the crowd on his way to the pulpit when he heard a mother advise her daughter: “My daughter, keep your veil on. Show your beauty to no one, lest it afterward be despised.” Shaykh Ruzbihan stopped and said: “O woman!

“Beauty cannot bear to be shut away in solitude. Its whole desire is to be joined with love, for from before eternity Beauty and Love exchanged a promise never to part.” (Their separation, as we may recall, supplied the dramatic impulse of Suhrawardi's Vade Mecum of the Faithful of Love; see above, Book II, Chapter VII, section 3.) The later pages of Ruzbihan's Spiritual Diary show him living in familiar intimacy with faces of heavenly beauty. The words he uses to describe them will reappear when he tells us how the faces of earthly beauty look to him.

Another episode reveals the private anguish that every vision of beauty awakens in Ruzbihan's heart: the meeting of attainment with the unattainable; the vision withheld within the vision granted; absence tasted in presence; the longing for something still beyond, even within the peace sometimes tasted here below. Moment after moment, through this coexistence of opposites, the soul makes its Return, and there is no respite.

Ruzbihan himself speaks of this during his final illness. He had been struck by a form of paralysis affecting one side of his body. Far from wanting to cure it, he seemed almost to wish the illness would grow worse. Without telling him, one of his disciples traveled to Cairo and obtained from the royal treasury a quantity of balm intended to heal the shaykh. When the disciple returned to Shiraz and presented himself before Ruzbihan, he heard these words: “My child, may God reward your good intentions!
“But now, go to the gate of the khanqah. A poor mangy dog lies there. Rub this balm on him; perhaps it will do him some good.

“But know that Ruzbihan's suffering is not the kind that can be eased with a balm from this world. It is one of the chains of love that God has fastened around his foot, and there it will remain until he reaches the happiness of meeting Him.”

It was only natural that someone so deeply moved by feeling should also be a musician, and should embrace the practice of the spiritual concert, or sama', which many other Sufis regarded with suspicion. Ruzbihan was an ardent practitioner until the last years of his life.

But then he no longer needed the mediation of audible sounds: what cannot be heard began to make itself heard within him as pure inner music. He gave this explanation to a friend who asked why he had stopped attending the gatherings: “From now on,” he said, “it is God Himself, in person, who is the oratorio I listen to. I refrain from listening to any other music but Him.”

It was as though Ruzbihan could even, beyond the grave, share with one of his dearest friends and disciples the gathering of voices beyond the senses that he heard within the oratorio of his soul. That disciple, Shaykh Abu Bakr ibn Taher Hafez, was especially inconsolable after Ruzbihan's departure. He himself tells this story: “Every morning at dawn, Shaykh Ruzbihan and I would take turns reciting the Quran aloud. He would chant about ten verses, and I would chant the next ten. When he had gone, I felt trapped in an anguish of grief.

“Toward the end of the night I would rise and perform the Prayer. Then I would go and sit beside his grave, and there I would begin chanting the Quran, my tears flowing as I suffered the pain of being left alone, separated from him. One morning, suddenly, I heard the shaykh's voice. It seemed to rise from the grave; and there it was, chanting the verses of the Book with me, ten at a time, as we had always done. This continued until the Companions gathered, and then the voice stopped.
“But the same thing happened on the following days, and so it went on for some time. Then one day I told a friend about it. From that day onward, I never heard the shaykh's voice again...”

III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
We can begin to understand the suffering Rûzbehân spoke of when he told his over-devoted disciple that it was not among the pains “that can be soothed with a balm from this world.”
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil

The key lies in a short treatise that sets out the ideas we need in order to understand another of his works, devoted entirely to the transformation of human love into divine love. This transformation takes place not so much in the beloved as in the lover. It is a change in the way one sees, and it opens the way to tawhîd in its esoteric sense: the inward realization of divine unity.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil

Rûzbehân called the short treatise “An Explanation of the Veils and Screens in the Spiritual Dwelling Places of the Mystics,” or simply the “Book of the Clouding.” Its inspiration came one night when he awoke and heard, within his heart, a summons from the divine Friend. He was to write about the hidden meaning of the Veils that come between the Friend and those devoted to Him: the stages of their mystical journey, the spiritual states through which they pass, and the divine Attributes that appear to them as manifestations of light. His purpose was to warn them of the snares and dangers along the way, and to help them perceive and recognize the miracle quietly taking place within themselves.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil

Rûzbehân takes as his guiding theme a saying attributed to the Prophet: “A cloud passes over my heart; indeed, I ask God's forgiveness for it seventy times a day.” A second saying explains the first: “For prophets and the friends of God (Awliyâ), there is a clouding of the innermost consciousness (sirr, the ‘secret’) and a veiling of the lights. This is the ordeal through which God makes them pass”—the ordeal of the Veil.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil

In some forty pages of extraordinary intensity, Rûzbehân's meditation produces something like a theosophy of Spirit, a wisdom concerned with divine reality. In our own vocabulary we might call it a phenomenology of Spirit, provided we do not import our modern “sense of history” into it. What matters here is its understanding of Spirit, centered entirely on its understanding of prophecy.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil

As in much Sufi theosophy, Rûzbehân begins his account of creation with a famous tradition in which the Divine Being declares that He was a Hidden Treasure longing to be known, and that He brought creation into existence in order to be known and to know Himself in His creatures.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil

The first reality in Rûzbehân's account is neither the First Intellect of the philosophers who followed Avicenna, nor Nafas al-Rahmân, the Breath of the Compassionate, as in Ibn ‘Arabî. It is Spirit. Through the primordial bringing-into-being of Spirit, all the “Holy Spirits” subsist: the spiritual individualities that have existed from before time, the beings who make up the “offspring of the most sacred Light.”
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil

To these Holy Spirits the primordial divine Light made itself known in a mysterious scene beyond the beginning of time. Through them, the Light put a question to itself: “Am I not your Lord?” And they answered with one voice. It was for these Holy Spirits that the Veils were created, to become their ordeal. Their descent into earthly life, the mission for which they are sent here, has no other purpose than to lead them through that ordeal to victory.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
But if the ordeal of the Veil contains the very meaning of creation, it also betrays a hidden anguish within God Himself.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
The first veil is simply the condition of these Holy Spirits as beings.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil

We must not imagine a sequence of events measured by ordinary time, yet we have to say that “at first” they did not exist, and “then” they were called into being. Rûzbehân shares here a premise of the Avicennian philosophers: beings do not possess within themselves what is needed to exist. Only the One possesses, in Himself, all that is needed to be what He is.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil

“I am not saying,” Rûzbehân writes, “that nonbeing is something. I am saying that the eternal priority of their nonbeing”—a priority that is therefore eternally present—“is, for that subtle reality (latîfa) which is Spirit, the first of the Veils.” From this Veil, we might say, all the others arise. It is the source of every misunderstanding about who truly acts whenever anything comes into being. Here, then, is the very origin of the ordeal of the Veil.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil

Rûzbehân now offers an extraordinary insight. Every distinct particle of being within the subtle reality of primordial Spirit comes into existence through a divine self-disclosure, a theophany that reveals one of God's Attributes—as though God, in an ecstasy of love, were revealing Himself to Himself.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
Thus every particle of being is an eye (‘ayn) opened by His light, an eye wholly absorbed in contemplating the Light from which it came.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil

But now God experiences jealousy toward Himself. By making Himself visible to Himself, by revealing Himself, He is no longer simply His own witness. There is a Witness (shâhid) “outside” Him, someone “other” than Himself. In this jealousy, as though seeking to reclaim Himself from Himself, God turns the eye of Spirit—His first subtle creation—away from contemplating Him, and directs the creature instead toward contemplating itself. “Then it contemplated itself and became absent [or was hidden, ghaybat] from the contemplation of the original Being. And this vision of itself by itself became its second Veil.”
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
The second Veil thus grows out of the first: the very fact of being a creature. Here the crucial idea of the “witness of contemplation” (shâhid; see Chapter V below) begins to take shape.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil

We can already see that being sent back to self-knowledge is the ordeal above all others. One emerges victorious only when the famous saying has become a truth verified in one's own experience: “Whoever knows himself knows his Lord.” Victory will put an end to the divine jealousy of love, which meanwhile sets the worlds in motion. God wants to be known by a Witness, but that Witness can be none other than Himself. To recognize this identity, the Witness must undergo the same ordeal again and again.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil

Divine jealousy tries to lead him astray, to make him turn his gaze away from God and toward himself as though toward something separate, forgetting that, if he witnesses the divine acts of contemplation, it is because he is the very “eye” through which God contemplates Himself. That is why the Divine Being reveals Himself through His supreme Attribute, Beauty.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil

He brings forth the invisible worlds, the worlds of mystery, and appears within them in Adamic form, as the heavenly Human Being. He brings forth the worlds of becoming, then the microcosm of earthly humanity, with its subtle spiritual physiology centered on the heart, and finally the bodily and psychic organs, with their inner and outer senses. Each stage, each field of perception opening before its corresponding faculty, becomes a Veil for Spirit as it descends from one level to the next.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil

Each offers a fresh temptation to “look away” from the true object of contemplation and desire. And when Spirit, during its earthly journey, begins to ascend and return to its origin, each new station or spiritual dwelling place (maqâmât) raises another veil between it and its true goal. Here Rûzbehân shows the psychological insight of the greatest spiritual masters. In the end he identifies seventy Veils, thereby suggesting an explanation for the Prophet's words: “A cloud passes over my heart; I ask God's forgiveness for it seventy times a day.”
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
In Rûzbehân's language, divine jealousy as the cause of the heart's clouding means this: God can be reached only through His revelations, His theophanies.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil

Yet when those theophanies are perceived by a gaze other than His own—a gaze conscious of itself as separate—they become something other than Him. And this, with consequences of immeasurable importance, is precisely what outward tawhîd does: the monotheism of official religion, of Islam understood only in its literal sense.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil

For the Sufi, monotheism amounts to the worst kind of metaphysical idolatry so long as the believer has not attained the mystic's awareness: the knowledge that one's own gaze is the gaze through which God contemplates Himself, and one's own testimony the testimony through which He bears witness to Himself.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil

Unfortunately, official theologians call this monism or pantheism. Whatever their misunderstanding, the theophany remains both a veil and an ordeal. God appears as though to turn our attention away from Him; we then seek Him beyond the Veil, until we experience what Rûzbehân calls the “madness of the unattainable.”
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil

But we triumph over the ordeal when the veil has become a mirror. Then we must look into that mirror, and nowhere else, because what it reveals is visible nowhere else. The contradiction is overcome. The theophany, the beautiful face, does not draw us away from uncreated Beauty, for it reveals that Beauty. The mystic follows the Prophet's example: “His gaze neither swerved nor overstepped” (53:17). He neither swerves by looking at the mirror without seeing what appears within it, nor oversteps by seeking elsewhere what wishes to reveal itself here.
